title: Philippine Ecosystems

standard_text: Philippine ecosystems: forests, mangroves, coral reefs, seagrass beds, wetlands and agricultural ecosystems; energy flow and nutrient cycles; biodiversity, endemic species and conservation. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 2)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 2): Philippine ecosystems, energy flow, nutrient cycles, biodiversity and conservation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The Philippines is a megadiverse country.
key_sub: Energy flows and matter cycles in ecosystems.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Philippines has tropical rainforests, mossy forests, grasslands, mangroves, coral reefs in the Coral Triangle, seagrass beds, lakes and rivers, and rice terraces. Many species, such as the Philippine eagle and tarsier, are endemic.

In every ecosystem, energy flows from producers to consumers and is lost as heat, while carbon, nitrogen and water are recycled. Deforestation, destructive fishing, pollution and climate change threaten Philippine ecosystems; protected areas and sustainable practices conserve them.

Example

Which ecosystem shelters young fish among its roots?

Coastal trees

Answer: mangroves

Example

What is an endemic species?

Found in one place only

Answer: a species found naturally only in one place

Common mistakes

  • Thinking energy is recycled.
  • Thinking coral reefs are rocks with no life.
  • Thinking losing one species does not matter.

faq.q: Why are marine protected areas important?
faq.a: They let fish and corals recover, which helps nearby fisheries.

faq.q: Why plant native trees instead of exotic ones?
faq.a: Native trees support native wildlife and suit local conditions.

items.q: A hurricane knocks down trees; soil and seeds remain. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Which human activity harms coral reefs?
items.e: Blasts and poison destroy corals.

items.q: A glacier melts back and leaves bare rock. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Which interaction is shown when a lyrebird and a bandicoot both dig in the leaf litter for the same insects?
items.e: Two species use the same limited resource.

items.q: Loggers clear a forest, and shrubs grow back. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: What is a tropical rainforest?
c: a cold forest of pine trees only
a warm, wet forest with tall trees and very high biodiversity
items.e: Philippine rainforests are home to the Philippine eagle.

items.q: Which Philippine ecosystem has trees whose roots grow in salty water along the coast?
items.e: Mangroves grow between land and sea.

items.q: A forest fire burns trees but leaves the soil. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Why are mangroves called nurseries of the sea?
c: they grow in the open ocean
young fish, crabs and shrimp grow up safely among their roots
items.e: Mangrove roots give shelter.

items.q: A remora fish attaches to a shark and eats scraps of its food; the shark is not affected. What is this relationship?
items.e: One benefits, the other is unaffected.

items.q: Which factor is density-independent?
c: predation that increases with prey numbers
disease spreading through a crowded colony
items.e: Drought affects a population whatever its density.

items.q: A farm field is abandoned and weeds move in. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Which protected reef in the Sulu Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
items.e: It has a very high diversity of marine life.

items.q: What is a keystone species?
c: the largest species in a food web
a species whose effect on its ecosystem is much larger than its numbers suggest
a species found only in one place
the most common species in an ecosystem
items.e: Removing it changes the whole community.

items.q: A predator–prey graph shows the predator population peaking after the prey population. Why?
c: the two populations are not linked
predators increase only after there is plenty of prey, then fall when prey run short
items.e: The cycles are linked but out of step.

items.q: What is the carrying capacity of an environment?
c: the fastest rate at which a population can grow
the number of species it contains
the largest population it can support for a long time
items.e: Limited by food, water, space and other resources.

items.q: Which is a freshwater ecosystem?
c: a mangrove forest by the sea
items.e: Lakes and rivers are freshwater ecosystems.

items.q: What is a seagrass bed?
c: an underwater meadow of flowering plants in shallow seas, where dugongs and fish feed
items.e: Seagrass also traps sediment and stores carbon.

items.q: What is secondary succession?
c: a food chain with two consumers
regrowth of a community where soil remains after a disturbance such as fire
items.e: It is faster because soil and seeds are already there.

items.q: Why are coral reefs important?
c: they are made of plants only
they are home to many fish and protect coasts from waves
items.e: The Tubbataha Reefs are a protected marine park.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 20 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 20 × 10³ = 20,000 J.

items.q: Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
c: much is used in respiration and released as heat, and some is in undigested waste
energy is destroyed at each level
all the energy is stored as biomass
items.e: Typically only about 10% passes to the next level.

items.q: The producers contain 20,000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the primary consumers contain 1,600 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 8.00%.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 40 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 40 × 10³ = 40,000 J.

items.q: The primary consumers contain 12,000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the secondary consumers contain 600 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 5.00%.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 90 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 90 × 10³ = 90,000 J.

items.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five links?
c: plants cannot support more than one consumer
there is too much biomass at the top
too little energy is left at the top to support another level
items.e: Energy decreases at each trophic level.

items.q: In a food web, what happens to the number of crickets if most of the frogs that eat them are removed?
items.e: Less predation lets the prey population grow.

items.q: A single eucalyptus supports thousands of caterpillars. What shape is the pyramid of numbers?
c: inverted at the base (one producer, many consumers)
items.e: Pyramids of numbers can be inverted; pyramids of energy cannot.

items.q: Which process returns nutrients from dead organisms to the soil?
items.e: Decomposers recycle matter, not energy.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 70 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 70 × 10³ = 70,000 J.

items.q: What does a pyramid of biomass show?
c: the number of organisms at each level
the dry mass of organisms at each trophic level
items.e: Biomass is measured per unit area.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 10 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 10 × 10³ = 10,000 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 3,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 3,000 × 0.12 = 30.0 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 4,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 4,000 × 0.13 = 4.00 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 900,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 900,000 × 0.13 = 900 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 60 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 60 × 10³ = 60,000 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 50 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 50 × 10³ = 50,000 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 30 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 30 × 10³ = 30,000 J.

items.q: Which statement about matter and energy in ecosystems is correct?
c: energy is recycled, but matter is lost
matter is recycled, but energy flows through and is lost as heat
items.e: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

items.q: Which processes return carbon to the air?
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon from the air dissolves into the ocean. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon in coal returns to the air at a power station. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Kenneth observes: “A dead tree rots on the forest floor.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from producers into consumers?
items.e: Animals eating plants.

items.q: Kevin observes: “A leaf falls and decomposers break it down.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Where does animals eating plants move carbon?
c: from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
items.e: Animals eating plants moves carbon from producers into consumers.

items.q: Where does shell-building sea animals forming limestone move carbon?
c: from the atmosphere into living things
from dead organisms into the geosphere
from the hydrosphere into the geosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
items.e: Shell-building sea animals forming limestone moves carbon from the hydrosphere into the geosphere.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere?
items.e: Volcanic eruptions.

items.q: Where does formation of fossil fuels over millions of years move carbon?
c: from dead organisms into the geosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
items.e: Formation of fossil fuels over millions of years moves carbon from dead organisms into the geosphere.

items.q: Mark observes: “Bacteria in soil change nitrogen into a form plants can use.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from living things into the atmosphere?
c: formation of fossil fuels over millions of years
items.e: Forest fires.

items.q: What happens to the carbon in a dead tree?
c: It stays in the log forever.
Decomposers release it as CO<sub>2</sub>, which plants can use again.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Where do the atoms in your body come from?
c: from the food you eat, which came from plants and the air
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Where does photosynthesis move carbon?
c: from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
from the atmosphere into living things
from living things into the atmosphere
items.e: Photosynthesis moves carbon from the atmosphere into living things.

items.q: Is energy recycled in an ecosystem?
c: No. Energy flows through and leaves as heat; matter is recycled.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Christian observes: “Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: In a swamp with little oxygen, how do some bacteria break down matter?
c: anaerobic respiration, which can release methane
they cannot break it down at all
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Which process puts carbon from the air into living things?
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Where does ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub> move carbon?
c: from the atmosphere into living things
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
items.e: Ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub> moves carbon from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere.

items.q: What happens to an ecosystem when one species disappears?
c: the food web changes and other species may be affected
the ecosystem becomes a desert at once
items.e: Living things depend on one another.

items.q: What is ecosystem diversity?
c: the number of species in one quadrat
the size of the largest ecosystem
the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in a region
the variety of alleles in one species
items.e: A region with reef, mangrove and seagrass has high ecosystem diversity.

items.q: Why should forests on mountains be protected?
c: they hold soil, prevent landslides and keep water in watersheds
items.e: Watersheds supply water to towns.

items.q: Which population is most at risk from a new disease?
c: a large population with many alleles
a population of a widespread species
a small, inbred population with low genetic diversity
items.e: Tasmanian devils have low genetic diversity, which helped facial tumor disease spread.

items.q: Tasmanian devils have very low genetic diversity. Why has this made devil facial tumor disease worse?
c: low diversity makes them grow too fast
their immune systems do not recognize tumor cells from other devils as foreign
the disease is caused by a mutation in the climate
items.e: Similar genes mean the tumor cells are not rejected.

items.q: Which ecosystem is found at the top of high mountains like Mount Pulag?
items.e: It is cooler and wetter high in the mountains.

items.q: Which is a way to protect Philippine ecosystems?
c: planting native trees and mangroves and not throwing garbage in rivers
items.e: Small actions add up.

items.q: Two sites each have 5 species. At site An each species has about 20 individuals; at site B one species has 90 and the rest have 2 or 3. Which is more diverse?
c: they are equally diverse because richness is the same
site A, because it has the same richness and higher evenness
site B, because dominance means a healthier community
site B, because it has more individuals of one species
items.e: Same richness, higher evenness = higher diversity.

items.q: What is coral bleaching?
c: corals turn white when warm water makes them lose their algae
items.e: Bleached corals may die if the water stays warm.

items.q: Which describes a marine protected area (MPA)?
c: a place where reefs are blasted
a port for big ships only
a part of the sea where fishing and other activities are limited to let marine life recover
items.e: Fish populations grow inside MPAs and spill over.

items.q: Which ecosystem forms the famous rice terraces of Ifugao?
c: an agricultural ecosystem carved into mountain slopes
items.e: The terraces are fed by water from mountain forests.

items.q: What is an endemic species?
c: a species found naturally in only one place
a species that has died out
items.e: The tarsier and the Philippine eagle are endemic to the Philippines.

items.q: What does ‘ecosystem services’ mean?
c: the number of species in an ecosystem
money paid to visit a national park
the benefits people get from ecosystems, such as clean water, pollination and food
items.e: Mangroves protect coasts and act as fish nurseries.

items.q: What is biodiversity?
c: the total mass of plants in an ecosystem
the variety of life at the genetic, species and ecosystem levels
the number of animals in an area
the number of endangered species in a country
items.e: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.

items.q: Why are the Philippines called a megadiverse country?
c: it has a very large number of species, many found nowhere else
items.e: Many species are endemic to the Philippine islands.

items.q: What is species richness?
c: the number of different species in an area
how evenly individuals are spread among species
items.e: Richness counts species; evenness compares their numbers.

items.q: What is genetic diversity?
c: the variety of alleles and genes within a species
the number of different species in an area
the variety of habitats in a region
the number of individuals in a population
items.e: Genetic diversity is variation inside one species.

items.q: What does the species–area relationship of Alexander von Humboldt state?
c: species richness increases with area, but only up to a limit
items.e: log S = log C + Z log A.

items.q: Why is high genetic diversity important to a population?
c: it increases the population's size immediately
some individuals are more likely to survive a new disease or change
items.e: Variation is the raw material for natural selection.

items.q: Why are wetlands important?
c: they filter water, hold floodwater and are habitats for birds and fish
items.e: The Olango Island wetlands host migratory birds.

items.q: Diane observes: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” What impact can this have?
c: air pollution and more carbon dioxide
algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Trisha wants to know whether a new bus line reduces air pollution. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: measure air quality and traffic for several months before and after
ask one neighbor what they think
check once on a single day
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Diane wants to know whether a recycling program reduces garbage. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: check once on a single day
ask one neighbor what they think
weigh the garbage sent to the landfill each week before and after
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Christian reads: “A flood covers a river valley with mud.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Kristine observes: “Fertilizer runs off farms into a river.” What impact can this have?
c: algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Kenneth observes: “Rainwater carries oil and garbage from car parks into streams.” What impact can this have?
c: animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Camille wants to know whether a rain garden reduces stream pollution. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: ask one neighbor what they think
check once on a single day
measure pollution in the stream before and after the rain garden is built
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Isabel wants to know whether a wildlife bridge reduces animal deaths. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: count animals hit on the road before and after the bridge
check once on a single day
ask one neighbor what they think
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Jericho reads: “Hunters remove most of the sea otters from a coast.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Lorna wants to know whether fewer fish die after a farm uses less fertilizer. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: check once on a single day
count fish and measure oxygen in the river over several years
ask one neighbor what they think
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Jenny observes: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” What impact can this have?
c: warmer water with less oxygen for fish
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Kristine's class studies this problem: “A factory releases hot water into a lake.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
cooling the water in ponds before it is released
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Mae reads: “A volcano covers land with ash.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Rose reads: “A long drought dries up streams.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Rose learns: A drought dried a pond. What happened to the frogs?
c: They moved into the trees permanently.
They decreased because they lost water and food.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Sheila's class studies this problem: “Fertilizer runs off farms into a river.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertilizer
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Bryan reads: “Wolves are returned to a national park.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Hazel's class studies this problem: “Rainwater carries oil and garbage from car parks into streams.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertilizer
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
rain gardens and permeable sidewalk that soak up runoff
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Kenneth learns: Wolves returned to Yellowstone. What happened to the elk?
c: They decreased, and willow trees along rivers grew back.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Emmanuel's class studies this problem: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertilizer
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.
